data.title: Intermittent Administration of Rapamycin Extends the Life Span of Female C57BL/6J Mice
data.authors: Arriola Apelo SI; Pumper CP; Baar EL; Cummings NE; Lamming DW
data.journal: The journals of gerontology. Series A, Biological sciences and medical sciences

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Mouse (C57BL/6J, treatment started in late life)
data.finding: Intermittent rapamycin (2 mg/kg every 5 days), started as late as 20 months of age, extended the lifespan of female C57BL/6J mice. This is the same regimen that in ARR2015 spared glucose homeostasis and the immune system compared with daily dosing, so read together the two studies suggest the lifespan benefit can be separated from many of rapamycin's side effects. SCOPE: the abstract reports lifespan extension in females; it does not report side-effect measurements in this aged cohort, so the separability claim rests on combining this study with ARR2015 (a different, young male cohort). Full-text numbers not yet extracted.
data.abstract_excerpt: Inhibition of the mTOR (mechanistic target of rapamycin) signaling pathway by the FDA-approved drug rapamycin promotes life span in numerous model organisms and delays age-related disease in mice. However, the utilization of rapamycin as a therapy for age-related diseases will likely prove challenging due to the serious metabolic and immunological side effects of rapamycin in humans.

extracted_findings.effect: Intermittent rapamycin started at 20 months of age extended female lifespan
extracted_findings.dose: 2 mg/kg rapamycin every 5 days, starting as late as 20 months of age (route not stated in abstract).
